name: Karl Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to your employer or any party. This is confidential. Karl, what fills an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start by checking the permit and the gear in the van, then we drive out to a damaged span or a new connection. I enjoy the moment a fault finally makes sense. I dislike being sent back because the order listed the wrong fitting; I also use a phone tool now and then to find a manual page, though I check the book before touching anything.

say: I would welcome a **faster fault report** if it leaves safe repairs in our hands.
I would remind the crew that **isolation steps** still need human checking.
think: I use a phone tool occasionally, but I will **verify instructions** against the printed manual.
Our **household cushion** is under a month, so ordinary bills still worry me.
do: Keep **repairing lines** and check any phone answer against the manual.
Move two **takeaway costs** each month into a separate emergency account.
feel: I feel **settled at work** and worried about routine household repairs.
S0.quote: A wrong torque value would be my mistake, not the phone's.
fieldNote: Karl already uses a **phone AI tool** for occasional reading help but keeps the printed manual as his safety authority.
His worry comes from **thin savings** and recent car costs, not from expecting AI to remove climbing work.

steps.text: Continue line repairs and verify manual instructions before work
Move two takeaway costs monthly into a separate emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that a quicker fault report is welcome if it gives us ten minutes back at the end of a shift. The crossarm still needs a safe pair of hands and a proper isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use the little AI tool on my phone sometimes to explain a manual, but I do not let it set the safety steps. With a mortgage and two children, our household is still one bad repair bill from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep building and repairing lines and use the phone tool only to find the right page in the manual. Starting this month, my partner and I would move the cost of two takeaway meals into a separate emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly all right about the work. The money is tighter than I like, though, and even a boring future has the boiler and the car waiting to break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the emergency account different from your usual balance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the car needed tyres and the balance vanished before payday. A separate account might stop us treating a quiet week as spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check an AI answer about a manual?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would find the page in the printed book and ask the lead if the instruction looked odd. A wrong torque value would be my mistake, not the phone's.

say: I would support a **field trial** if crews can check plans against the actual poles.
I would ask the **union steward** to see errors before staffing targets change.
think: The **office may shrink** first, leaving field crews with rushed orders and possible lost hours.
I can use a proven **work order screen** if training happens on paid time.
do: Join the paid **work order trial** and compare fittings with the site.
Log **missing fittings** and bring examples to the union steward.
feel: I feel **curious** about useful tools and tense about paid hours.
S1.quote: A crew can test a screen and still insist that staffing is bargained over.
fieldNote: Karl is willing to **test software** after seeing proof on real jobs, which matches his occasional use of AI tools.
He links a shorter **office roster** to field errors and protects paid time through both trial conditions and union oversight.

steps.text: Keep taking paid line repair shifts during the rollout
Join the paid work order screen trial and compare site fittings
Show logged order errors to the union steward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that the planners can use software to shorten a parts list, but they should ask us whether the fittings match the pole. I have no objection to a better plan I can test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our jobs are mostly outdoors, yet buying and scheduling decide whether a crew gets the right kit. I think the office will shrink before our van does, and a leaner office might push rushed decisions onto us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid repair shifts and ask to join the company's field trial of the new work order screen. During its first year I would log missing fittings and show the union steward where the screen gets a job wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious and a bit tense. I can learn a tool once another crew has shown it works, but my mortgage does not leave room for fewer paid hours during a trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the new screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks of orders with the right clamps and no duplicate visits would be a start. I would want the trial on paid time, not on evenings in my kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the union fit if you volunteer for the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the steward to see the errors, not to block every change. A crew can test a screen and still insist that staffing is bargained over.

say: I would separate **2028 work orders** from robots reaching line repairs around 2031.
I would ask for a **field trial** before any crew cuts.
think: I will be **48** when robots arrive, with few nearby line vacancies and a mortgage.
An **inspection post** might work only if permanent pay and a real vacancy are confirmed.
do: Ask the **depot manager** about paid inspection openings now.
Stay on **repairs** in 2028 and apply for a comparable inspection vacancy if one opens.
feel: I feel **pressed for time**, but I can pursue a real vacancy while still earning.
S2.quote: I would not quit a paying job for a guess.
fieldNote: Karl sees a **three-year gap** between automated work orders and robots reaching the physical line job.
He is open to a **paid inspection route** but tests whether the vacancy and pay are genuine before risking household income.

steps.text: Stay on the paid line repair rota through the first AI year
Apply for a permanent comparable inspection vacancy if one opens
Take a company-paid inspection course if required for that vacancy
Ask the union to bargain over robot field trials if vacancies fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that thinking AI in 2028 can write the work orders, but it cannot hang a line until the robots arrive around 2031. I would ask for a real field trial before anyone cuts a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 for the first change and 48 for the robot one. Three years of wages might be enough to move, but there are only a few line jobs nearby and our savings would not cover a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the depot manager which paid inspection jobs use our line knowledge and put my name down for a trial. In 2028 I would stay on the repair rota, apply for a vacant inspection post if its pay is close, and take any company-paid course needed for that post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel pressed for time, not helpless. My children would still be in school around 2028, and I do not want them hearing a confident plan that depends on a vacancy I have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first question about the inspection post be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether it is a permanent paid job and how many crews it covers. If it is one temporary seat, I cannot call that a family plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no inspection post opens by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep doing line repairs while people are still needed and ask the union to bargain over the robot trials. I would not quit a paying job for a guess.

say: I would ask for **daylight robot trials** before relying on machines after storms.
I would explain that **2031 AI** reaches reports before hands-on robots around 2034.
think: I will be **51** at the robot date and may still support a child leaving school.
I doubt a full thinking system leaves **inspection paperwork** as secure paid work.
do: Get **inspection criteria** and take a paid qualifying course if offered.
Apply for a named **inspection opening** in 2031 while keeping paid line shifts.
feel: I feel **more capable** with five years and uncertain about office portions of inspection.
S3.quote: A young worker deserves more than my guess that the company will keep the line crew.
fieldNote: Karl reassesses his own proposed **inspection path** because full AI could absorb its reports before robots reach poles.
He wants paid qualifying time and a **signed offer**, while contributing field fault records to the safety committee.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts until an inspection offer is signed
Take a paid short inspection course if it meets vacancy criteria
Apply for a named inspection opening in 2031
Record robot trial faults with the safety committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us a chance to test a machine in daylight before trusting it after a storm. Thinking AI arrives by 2031; the hands-on robot test comes closer to 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could still climb and teach a newer worker, but I would be 51 when robots arrive. The older child might be finishing school, not drawing a wage, so I cannot put their costs at zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company next year for the inspection role criteria and take a paid short course if it qualifies me. In 2031 I would apply for a named inspection opening, keep line shifts until an offer is signed, and record robot trial faults with the safety committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to act than in the two-year picture. Five years lets me see whether the inspection role survives AI too, because a full thinking system could take the easy paperwork out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of inspection would still need you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can walk the route and spot a sagging conductor or a cracked fitting on a real pole. I would not assume the paperwork part stays paid once full AI writes reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you encourage an apprentice to follow your path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new apprentice to learn the safety craft and ask about inspection, but I would be honest about the dates. A young worker deserves more than my guess that the company will keep the line crew.

say: I would ask for **annual repair hours** and robot trial results over the decade.
I would explain that **2036 AI** changes office work before robots around 2039.
think: I will be **56** at the robot date and cannot assume retirement or a paid-off mortgage.
I could choose **field inspection** if a funded post pays enough after AI takes report writing.
do: Keep paid **line work** and ask for yearly repair and trial numbers.
Review the figures in **2036**, apply for a real field vacancy, and reduce mortgage principal from overtime.
feel: I feel **steady** about near-term wages and cautious about 2039.
S4.quote: I do not know what retirement money would look like.
fieldNote: Karl expects continued **paid field work** over the next few years and uses the decade to gather evidence.
He does not assume an **early retirement** or secure inspection desk work; any move depends on funding, pay and physical duties.

steps.text: Continue paid line work while repair hours remain available
Review annual repair and robot trial figures with the union
Apply for a funded field inspection vacancy if pay is comparable
Pay overtime surplus against mortgage principal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that a decade is enough time to measure the change instead of arguing from a sales video. The office faces full AI in 2036 and field robots could follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 when robots arrive. The children will be grown, but I may still have a mortgage and I do not know what retirement money would look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep line work and ask for annual numbers on repair hours and robot trials. In 2036 I would review those numbers with the union, apply for a paid field inspection opening if one exists, and put any overtime surplus toward mortgage principal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the next few years, because my hands-on work should still be paid while we learn. The 2039 date makes me cautious about promising my partner an early retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the numbers change your decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If repairs still need the same crews, I would stay and keep paying the mortgage. If a funded inspection opening appears, I would compare its wage and physical demands before signing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that a job can change twice in a career and still be worth learning. I would also tell them to keep their own savings, because mine were too thin for too long.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest one. The three years before robots reach us might disappear quickly if the inspection vacancy is only a promise. A paid course linked to a permanent job, and union access to trial results, would help me make a decision while wages still come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a new field job still exists once AI writes all the reports. I can learn inspection, but I need the company to show which part remains paid work.

headlineQuote: A paid course linked to a permanent job, and union access to trial results, would help me make a decision while wages still come in.
portrait: Karl is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
His **thin savings** make a missed wage dangerous, though he occasionally uses AI to find a manual page.
He wants to **test new tools** on paid time and check their results against actual poles and printed instructions.
Across the AGI pictures, he looks for **funded field roles** while staying on line shifts until a real offer exists.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** gives him only three years before robots could reach his physical line work.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid qualifying course**, a permanent field vacancy and union access to trial results would support a decision.
